title: Advances in Bioacoustics Sensing and Signal Processing Technologies
categories: 软体机器人与人机交互

abstract.original: Abstract Driven by advances in flexible electronics, microfabrication, and artificial intelligence, bioacoustics is revolutionizing sensing and signal processing across health, ecology, and intelligent systems. This review systematically examines key progress in high-performance acoustic sensors (e.g., piezoelectric, triboelectric, MEMS) and acquisition schemes for multi-scale biological sounds, ranging from heart tones to plant stress emissions. Furthermore, we delve into advanced methodologies for acoustic signal preprocessing, feature extraction, and classification, with a particular emphasis on the powerful analytical capabilities of multimodal data fusion and deep learning algorithms in complex real-world scenarios. Crucially, although the sensing requirements and biological targets vary drastically across medical, ecological, and agricultural domains, this review establishes a unifying framework centered on the shared physical and algorithmic challenges of bioacoustic information flow. By juxtaposing these diverse fields, the potential strategies for the interdisciplinary integration of sensing methodologies are highlighted. We also critically assess the essential roles of acoustic physical modeling, standardized testing frameworks, and gold-standard databases in evaluating system performance. Finally, the review highlights cutting-edge applications of bioacoustics in human health monitoring, medical diagnostics, human-computer interaction, and precision agriculture. By synthesizing current technological convergences and outlining future trajectories, we provide a comprehensive perspective on the promising directions and pivotal challenges facing bioacoustics research.

In terrestrial animal behavior research, acoustic cameras demonstrate unique value. The ultrasonic vocalization camera system (USVCAM) system developed by Matsumoto constructs an ultrasonic vocalization localization model based on the phase-lag principle[156], combined with an improved overlapping vocalization segmentation algorithm, thereby reducing the localization error of mouse ultrasonic vocalizations (Figure 9(a)). This system successfully resolves the dynamic social vocalizations of ICR mice, providing a powerful tool for researching the mechanisms of social behavior.

In marine exploration, where traditional optical imaging is often constrained by turbid water and light attenuation, acoustic cameras serve as an ideal alternative by leveraging the favorable propagation characteristics of sound in water. Zhou proposed a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based superresolution reconstruction algorithm for acoustic images, substantially improving underwater target recognition capabilities and laying a technical foundation for applications such as marine debris identification and fish monitoring [157] (Figure 9(b)). Furthermore, researchers, including Garcia and Connolly, have utilized acoustic cameras coupled with CNN models to achieve efficient and automated fish detection and underwater biological monitoring [158, 159] (Figure 9(c) and (d)).

Furthermore, the applications of acoustic cameras have extended to the research of marine mammals, aquatic plants, and other aquatic animals. From behavioral surveys of harbor seals and biomass counting in deep scattering layers to tracking the distribution of marine mammals using passive acoustic monitoring techniques and to Rogissart’s real-time observations of winter aggregation behaviors in Hemimysis anomala (Figur 9(e))[160], acoustic cameras have provided new perspectives for acquiring high temporal-resolution data and deepening the understanding of biological behaviors.

In specialized and extreme environment monitoring, acoustic cameras effectively circumvent optical interference through their sound-to-image conversion mechanism, demonstrating irreplaceable technical advantages. With the deepening integration of artificial intelligence algorithms, acoustic cameras are evolving from mere localization tools into intelligent monitoring platforms, poised to continuously drive innovative applications in bioacoustics, industrial diagnostics, and ecological conservation.

4.3 Active ultrasonic probing and image analysis

Although ultrasonic signals fall within the bioacoustic frequency spectrum by physical definition, their acquisition and analytical paradigms differ fundamentally from the passive listening techniques discussed in the preceding sections. Bioacoustic monitoring of animal vocalizations, cardiopulmonary sounds, and other physiological events primarily relies on passive listening to signals inherently generated by biological processes. In contrast, ultrasonic sensing typically employs active pulse-echo probing, in which the transducer actively emits high-frequency acoustic waves and detects the reflected echoes, combined with B-mode spatial image reconstruction. figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption_original: Figure 1. Overview of the origin, classification, and propagation of bioacoustic signals in biological species. (a) Origin and classification of sound. (b) Sound propagation in biological species. Depicts sound propagation characteristics and acoustic signal acquisition strategies across humans, animals, and plants. For humans, it includes vocal sounds from the throat (ranging from 20 to 2 kHz) and internal acoustic signals generated by organs such as the cardiopulmonary system, stomach, and bowel. For animals, it covers broadband acoustic signals utilized in sensing and communication. For plants (exemplified by tomatoes, etc.), it illustrates acoustic signal propagation within internal structures (e.g., xylem, cambium, phloem) and corresponding detection methods. Additionally, cross-sectional/profiled views (e.g., of the human thorax and plant tissues) visualize how acoustic signals propagate, reflect, and transmit in biological tissues.
